case_name: State of Karnataka v Amajappa and Others
facts: Eramma was married to A-1 and they were living in a hut in Sagar Camp. Some time before the incident, their relations soured and they started living separately in separate huts.
Hanamantappa died and then he married PW7 Mallamma about 3 years prior to the incident, but they could not pull on together and she went back to her parents' home.
At about 9.30 p.m. on 11.12.1989, A-1 and A-2 armed with axes and A-3 and A-4 armed with sticks came to the hut where Hanamantappa (D-2) was standing and started assaulting him.

Eramma (D-1) raised an alarm on which persons from the neighbourhood came there. Apprehending danger to her life, she tried to run away but the accused chased her and after catching hold assaulted her with axes and sticks, as a result of which she sustained injuries and died.
The incident was seen in the light of bulbs on the electric poles. Information was then conveyed to PW1 Mudakappa, who is father of D-2, who came to the scene of occurrence along with his wife.
issues: Whether the prosecution had established its case against the accused regarding commission of murder of Eramma and Hanamantappa
Whether the testimony of the eye-witnesses was trustworthy
petitioner_arguments: The prosecution examined 20 witnesses and filed some documentary evidence to establish its case.
The prosecution argued that the FIR is not silent as to who gave information to the complainant PW1 Mudakappa that it was the accused who had committed the murder of the two deceased.
respondent_arguments: The respondent/defending party argued that the testimony of the eye-witnesses was not trustworthy and the prosecution had failed to establish its case against the accused regarding commission of murder of Eramma.
The respondent/defending party pointed out that there was evidence to show that Eramma was a woman of loose character and had illicit connections with several other persons.
court_reasoning: The High Court held that the FIR is totally silent as to who gave information to the complainant PW1 Mudakappa that it was the accused who had committed the murder of the two deceased.

The High Court also placed reliance upon the testimony of PW2, where he stated that after hearing the commotion, he had gone to the spot, but he had not seen as to who had assaulted whom and had only seen the dead bodies lying there.
In fact, his categorical statement was that by the time he came out of his hut, everything was over and he had not told about the incident to anybody else.
holding: The appeal accordingly fails and is hereby dismissed.
